results.title: Econometric Sense: Intent to Treat, Instrumental Variables and LATE Made Simple(er)
results.content: *"Instrumental variable methods allow us to capture the causal effect of treatment on the treated in spite of the nonrandom compliance decisions made by participants in experiments....Use of randomly assigned intent to treat as an instrumental variable for treatment delivered eliminates this source of selection bias."*. This is often represented as: Z -> D -> Y where Z is the instrument or random assignment, D is an indicator for actually receiving the treatment, and Y is the outcome. **4) Non-zero causal effect of Z on D:** Being assigned to the treatment group is highly correlated with actually receiving the treatment i.e. when Z =1 then D is usually 1 as well. So an ITT analysis would simply be a comparison of outcomes for folks randomly assigned to treatment (Z = 1) vs those that were controls (Z = 0) regardless of compliance or non-compliance (determined by D). But, we also know that Z  (by definition of compliance and assumption 4) is correlated with actual treatment assignment D for the compliers.

results.title: Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) Calculator
results.content: Run this analysis with our Local Average Treatment Effect Calculator. The Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) estimates the causal effect of a treatment for the subpopulation of **compliers** — individuals who take the treatment when assigned to it and abstain when assigned to control. Identified through an instrumental variable (IV), LATE is the central estimand in randomized trials with imperfect compliance and in natural experiments with partial take-up. * LATE scales the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect by the compliance rate difference (Wald estimator). * It applies only to compliers — not to always-takers or never-takers. * A first-stage F-statistic below 10 signals a weak instrument and unreliable LATE estimates. The denominator \Delta\_c is the compliance rate in the treatment arm minus that in the control arm, equal to the proportion of compliers. The Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) is the causal effect of a treatment for the subpopulation of compliers — individuals whose treatment status is changed by the instrument.

results.title: ITT vs LATE: Estimating Causal Effects with IV in Experiments with Imperfect Compliance | Towards Data Science
results.content: Here we use the instrumental variables (IV) method to estimate the local average treatment effect, which is the causal effect of treatment among those who complied with the assignment ("compliers") - i.e., those who used the coupon because they were assigned to receive it. * The LATE estimates the effect of treatment by adjusting the impact of treatment assignment (ITT) for the compliance rate (the probability of using the coupon given that the customer was assigned). The instrumental variable (in this case, assignment to the treatment group) must be correlated with the endogenous variable whose effect on future purchases we want to measure (coupon usage). By applying the 2SLS method, we derive an unbiased estimate of the causal effect of coupon usage specifically for those who comply with the treatment, effectively filtering out the influence of random assignment. **LATE estimate using IV**: It represents the causal effect of coupon usage on future purchases among compliers (those who used the coupon because they received it).

results.title: ITT vs LATE: Estimating Causal Effects with IV in Experiments with Imperfect Compliance | by Robson Tigre | TDS Archive | Medium
results.content:
Title: ITT vs LATE: Estimating Causal Effects with IV in Experiments with Imperfect Compliance | by Robson Tigre | TDS Archive | Medium
* **Local average treatment effect (LATE)**: Estimates the effect of treatment among those who complied with the assignment — those who used the coupon because they were assigned to receive it. In our example, it compares the future average purchases of customers assigned to receive a coupon (treatment group) with those who were not (control group). This method is useful for understanding the effect of the assignment itself, but it may underestimate the treatment's impact, as it includes individuals who did not use the coupon. Here we use the instrumental variables (IV) method to estimate the local average treatment effect, which is the causal effect of treatment among those who complied with the assignment ("compliers") — i.e., those who used the coupon because they were assigned to receive it. * The LATE estimates the effect of treatment by adjusting the impact of treatment assignment (ITT) for the compliance rate (the probability of using the coupon given that the customer was assigned). The instrumental variable (in this case, assignment to the treatment group) must be correlated with the endogenous variable whose effect on future purchases we want to measure (coupon usage). 1. The LATE provides the causal effect only for "compliers" — customers who used the coupon because they received it, and this effect is specific to this group (local validity only). By applying the 2SLS method, we derive an unbiased estimate of the causal effect of coupon usage specifically for those who comply with the treatment, effectively filtering out the influence of random assignment. **ITT estimate**: It measures the average effect that offering a coupon has on customers' future purchases. **LATE estimate using IV**: It represents the causal effect of coupon usage on future purchases among compliers (those who used the coupon because they received it). In our example, the estimated LATE was close to $50 (see the second figure in subsection "Verifying assumptions"), indicating that customers who complied by using the coupon saw their future purchases increase by roughly $50 compared to what would have happened without the coupon. This result is larger than the ITT effect of R$17.89, as LATE focuses specifically on compliers, who are more likely to experience the true causal impact of using the coupon.
